en: Monster waves slam into container ships.
So why don't the stacked boxes just slide off?
Glue? Gravity? Take a guess.
I'm Max, and this is Max Wise.
The secret starts in the hold.
Below deck, boxes slide down steel rails.
So they can't drift sideways.
Up on deck, there are no rails.
So every box needs its own lock.
Look at a box's corner.
It's a solid steel block with oval holes.
Between two boxes sits a twistlock.
Its cone fits into both holes.
One twist turns it sideways, and the boxes are locked together.
Many ships use semi automatic twistlocks.
The top box presses down, and the lock snaps shut by itself.
To unload, a worker pulls a rod to release it.
Long steel lashing rods also tie the lower boxes to the ship.
Without them, a tall stack could tip over in a big roll.
Still, some boxes do fall.
In twenty twenty five, almost fifteen hundred were lost at sea.
That's out of roughly two hundred eighty million shipped.
And a lost box can float for a while, hiding just under the waves.
That makes it a danger for other boats.
So it's not glue, and it's not luck.
It's rails below, and twistlocks and lashings on top.
Stay curious!
